title: Lists in order: shopping, steps and talk points
intro: A list in order is the job pictures and places do best. The trick is the same for a shopping trip, the steps of a chore and the points of a talk: one picture for each item, one stop for each picture.
example: Shopping: your stops are the front door, the hall table, the stairs, the sofa and the kitchen sink. Oranges are juggled by the door, bread sits like a pillow on the hall table, soap bubbles pour down the stairs, a tin of beans is wedged in the sofa and a fish is swimming in the sink. Steps of a chore, such as setting up a tent: one stop for each step, with a picture of the action, such as a giant peg hammered into the hall table. Talk points: one stop for each point, and one keyword for each picture, such as 'budget' for a coin jar on the stairs.
steps: Pick a route you know well with as many stops as you have items, ideally 5 to 10.
Turn each item or step into one picture that is big, odd and moving. For a step, picture the action itself. For a talk point, picture one keyword.
Put the pictures on the stops, one for each. Walk the route once slowly, then once without stopping.
Close your eyes or look away, and say the list in order. Peek at your written copy only for the ones you lost, then make those pictures stranger or put them nearer to the stop.
Wipe the route in your mind when you are done so it is fresh for the next list.
review: For a shopping list, check once on the way to the shop. For steps and talk points, check after ten minutes, the next day and a week later.
caveat: Write the list down as well. The pictures are your second copy, not your only one. A short list with no time pressure is often best left on paper. The one study behind route methods tested one kind of list and does not show a better memory for everything.

title: Numbers: pictures, groups and your own image list
intro: There are three ways to hold a number you have been given: a picture for each digit, a picture for each pair (the Major System), or a rhyme word for each digit. Try them on your own numbers and keep the one you like. First, cut the number into groups.
example: A number given to you as 482915 becomes three groups of two: 48, 29 and 15. With the Major System you turn each pair into a word and a picture (the game's Week 14 to 17 lessons show how). With number-shape pictures, each single digit has a shape you can picture, such as a 2 that looks like a swan. With rhyme pegs, each number has a rhyming word, such as 'one is a bun'. Whichever you use, put the pictures on stops along a short route. Say the groups aloud in a beat when you rehearse: 48, 29, 15.
steps: Cut the number into groups of 2 to 4 digits. Chunks are easier to hold than a long string.
Turn each group into a picture, using the method you like for this kind of number.
Place the pictures on stops or link them in a short story.
Say the groups aloud in a steady beat, then walk the route and say the number again without looking.
Check against the real number and fix any picture that slipped.
review: Check after ten minutes, the next morning and a week later. Keep a written or saved copy of any number you really need.
caveat: Use it for numbers you can share and need exactly, such as dates, house numbers and a friend's phone number. Never use it for PINs, passwords, bank or card details, or door codes.

title: Five senses: give the picture more to hold
intro: A picture is easier to find again when it has more in it than how it looks. Add a sound, a feel, a smell, a taste or a movement. Each one is one more thing that can bring the picture back.
example: Your item is 'lemon'. Do not just see a yellow lemon. Hear it squirt, feel the cold waxy skin, smell the sharp zest and feel your mouth pucker. Put that on your stop: the lemon bursts on the front door with a loud pop and a sour mist that makes you blink.
steps: Make your picture of the item as usual.
Add two more senses to it: a sound, a feel, a smell, a taste or a movement. Pick the ones that come easily for this item.
Make it move or change, because a picture that does something is easier to hold than one that sits still.
Place it and check yourself later like any other picture.
review: Check it the same way as any other list: after ten minutes, the next day and a week later.
caveat: This is about giving each picture more ways to be found again. It does not mean you are a 'visual' or 'hearing' type. Use whichever sense gives the richest picture for each item, and see in your own scores whether it helps you.

title: Memory rhythms: say it in a beat
intro: Saying something aloud, in a steady beat, gives you one more thing to hold on to. It is a small help for numbers and for exact wording, and it costs nothing.
example: A number in groups of three or four, such as 482, 915, 603. Say it with a beat: 'four-eight-two (pause), nine-one-five (pause), six-oh-three (pause)'. Pause between the groups, and say the groups the same way every time. For a line of a poem, tap the beat of the words as you say it.
steps: Cut the number or line into groups of 3 or 4.
Say it aloud in a steady beat with a short pause between groups.
Say it again with your eyes closed, in the same beat.
Then put the pictures on the route as usual. The beat is a second cue, not a replacement.
review: Say it again after ten minutes, then the next day.
caveat: Do this out loud on your own, away from the Mnemos study screens, which stay quiet. A beat helps with order and exact wording and does not unlock anything special. If you cannot say it aloud, say it silently in your head or tap it on a table.

title: A job interview
intro: Prepare three or four short stories from your own experience, learn the interviewer's name, and keep a few questions of your own. Pictures can hold these in order so you can think about what you are saying instead of what comes next.
example: Your stories are 'the project I fixed', 'a time I helped a team member' and 'a time I learned something quickly'. Walk a route of five stops: front door, hall, kitchen, living room and bedroom. At the front door, a toolbox bursting open (the project I fixed). In the hall, two people carrying a heavy box together (helping). In the kitchen, a book cooking in a pan (learning quickly). At the living room, a sign with your first question on it, and at the bedroom, your second question. When you meet the interviewer, turn the name into a picture and join it to a feature in one scene, as you did in Month 3.
steps: Write down three or four stories that show what you have done. Give each a short title.
Write two or three questions you want to ask them.
Give each story and question one picture and one stop on a route you know.
Practise telling each story aloud, using the picture as a reminder of its title and the first thing you say. Do not learn the words.
On the day, when you meet the interviewer, turn their name into a picture and say their name once in the conversation.
review: Walk the route the evening before and once more an hour before. Keep a small card with the titles, in case you need it.
caveat: Preparation can help you keep your points in order. It does not decide how an interview goes. Stay yourself, listen to the question, and answer what was asked, even if that means leaving a prepared story out.

title: Mind Maps
intro: A Mind Map shows how a topic fits together: the topic in the middle, a few branches around it and a few short leaves on each branch. Drawing one helps you see the shape. What helps memory most is closing it and rebuilding it from memory.
example: The topic is 'Bread' in the middle. Branches: Ingredients, Steps, Tools, Problems. Under Ingredients, the leaves are flour, water, yeast, salt. Under Steps: mix, rise, shape, bake. Study the map for a few minutes. Then cover it and draw the middle and the four branch names from memory, and write the leaves you can, under the right branch. Look, and fix what you missed. This is the same shape as the Mind Map drill in Mnemos.
steps: Write the topic in the middle of a blank page.
Draw three to six branches, one for each big part of the topic. Give each branch a short name of one or two words.
Add two to four leaves to each branch, one to three words each. Use keywords, not sentences.
Study it for a few minutes, then turn the page over.
Redraw it blank from memory: the middle, the branch names, then the leaves. Compare, circle what you missed, and try again later.
For something you want to keep in order, also put the branches on stops in a palace, one branch for each stop.
review: Redraw it blank the next day, then a week later. Each blank redraw is a check, so you only need to look at the original when you get stuck.
caveat: A map shows how a topic fits together, and studies of maps find a benefit on average, with large differences between studies. One experiment found that testing yourself helped more than making a map. So make the map, then test yourself by redrawing it blank, because that is the part that helps. A map is for structured facts, not for understanding an argument.

title: Reading to find your key points: Skim, Pick, Keep
intro: Skimming means looking quickly at the headings, the first lines and the last lines to see what a text is about. It is a reading step, not a memory method. It helps you pick your key points. Keeping them is a separate job.
example: You have a five-page article about how bees make honey. Skim: spend two minutes on the headings and the first and last line of each section. Pick: choose five to nine key points, such as 'bees collect nectar', 'they pass it to hive bees', 'water is fanned off', 'cells are sealed with wax', 'honey is stored for winter'. Keep: one picture and one stop for each point, and one keyword (nectar, fan, wax). Check later without looking.
steps: Skim: look at the title, the headings and the first and last line of each part, for a short time. Ask what this is about.
Pick: choose 5 to 9 points you want to keep. Write each as one short sentence, then underline one keyword in it.
Read closely where you need to understand something. Skimming does not replace careful reading.
Keep: give each keyword one picture and one stop.
Check: close the text and say the points in order, using the stops. Look only for what you lost.
review: Check the next morning, then a week later. Retest yourself rather than reread: trying to recall tends to help more than looking at the text again.
caveat: Skimming helps you find the key points. It does not store them, it does not make you understand them, and it is not a way to learn faster. When it matters that you understand, read carefully. Pictures hold the points; understanding comes from thinking about them.

title: Keeping it: retrieve first, then look
intro: What makes a memory last is trying to bring it back after a gap, and then checking. This page puts that into one habit: Check Before You Look.
example: On Tuesday you made pictures for seven points. On Wednesday morning, before you open your notes, say the seven points aloud, from memory. Then look. Mark the ones you missed. On Sunday do it again, and a month from now do it a third time.
steps: Before you reread or look anything up, try to say or write what you know.
Then look, and mark what you missed or got wrong.
Fix the weak pictures: make them stranger, bigger or nearer to the stop.
Check again after a gap: tomorrow, a week later, a month later. The gap is part of what makes it work.
Let go of things you no longer need. A few things kept well beat many things kept badly.
review: Put the dates in your calendar when you learn something you really want to keep: day 1, day 7, day 30 and day 90.
caveat: Practice testing and spacing are among the best-supported findings about memory, but this habit does not tell you what is worth keeping, and it does not mean you will never forget. Forgetting is normal. Write down what matters as well.

title: A talk without notes
intro: A palace gives your main points a fixed order, so you can speak naturally while you walk through them in your head. For a work talk, a Roman Room is enough: one room, five points.
example: A Roman Room is a single room you know well, with a fixed order of stops: the door, the window, the desk, the shelf and the lamp. Your talk has five points. Point one, 'where we are now', is the door: a signpost swings open in the doorway. Point two, 'what went well', is the window: a golden sun shines in. Point three, 'what did not', is the desk: a cracked cup spills on the papers. Point four, 'what we will do', is the shelf: a toolbox on the top shelf. Point five, 'what I need from you', is the lamp: a hand shaking a hand under the light. You do not memorise sentences. Each picture reminds you of the point, and your own words do the rest.
steps: Decide on 5 points, or up to 9 for a longer talk. Write each as one short line with one keyword.
Choose one room or a short route, with one stop for each point, in a fixed order.
Make one strong picture for each keyword and put it on its stop.

Rehearse aloud while you walk the stops in your head. Say the points in your own words, in the same beat each time if it helps you keep the pace. Learn only your opening and closing lines word for word.
Keep a one-page Mind Map of the talk as a second copy: the title in the middle and one branch for each point.
On the day, walk the stops as you speak. If you lose your place, glance at the Mind Map or your card.
review: Rehearse the walk aloud the day before and once more an hour before. If the talk is a regular one, wipe the room and use it for the next.
caveat: This keeps your points in order. It does not make the content good, and it works best on points you understand. Keep a card in your pocket as a backup, and write your numbers and names down on it. The one study behind route methods tested one kind of list and does not show a better memory for everything.

title: Keep your own text
intro: Your Own Text is a tool for learning something word for word that you choose yourself: a verse, a poem, a speech, lines in a play (with Role mode, you learn your own part and the other parts are shown as cues). You paste it in. Mnemos cuts it into small pieces, hides it a little at a time, and asks you again after a day, a week, a month, three months and six months.
example: You paste a four-verse poem. Mnemos makes four sections. You read the first, then see only the first letter of each word, then only the start of each line, then a blank card. Tomorrow it asks for that verse before it offers a new one. A week later it asks again. If a line slips, it returns tomorrow and you look at it again.
steps: Copy your text from a source you trust, exactly as written. Mnemos cannot check it for you.
Learn one or two sections a day, working through Read, First letters, Line starts and Blank.
Come back when the app says a check is ready, and say or type the section from nothing.
review: Checks come at 1, 7, 30, 90 and 180 days for each section you have learned. Slipped lines come back the next day.
caveat: Your text stays on this device and is in your backup. Checks here never change your skills. Only a typed check that holds after a week or more earns a little Lumen, once for each check and inside the daily practice limit, because only you can tell whether your text was right. Pictures are optional. If you learn better by sound and repetition, skip them.

title: A text you treasure
intro: People learn texts by heart because they matter to them: a poem, a verse, a speech, a family saying, a vow. Many communities have their own long-established ways of doing it, usually with a teacher or a group. Mnemos does not replace any of that. It is a practice aid. It can keep your place, hide and show your text a little at a time, and remind you when to check yourself again.
example: A learner copies two verses from an edition their teacher recommends into Your Own Text. They read the first verse aloud, then see only its first letters and say it again, then cover it and say it from nothing. Tomorrow the app asks for those verses before anything new. A week later it asks again. Then they say them to their teacher, who can hear what a screen cannot.
steps: Copy your text word for word from a printed or trusted edition. Mnemos cannot tell whether it is right, so check it with your teacher or a source you trust before you start.
Let the tool cut it into small pieces. Say each piece aloud, then with only first letters, then from nothing. Skip pictures if you prefer to learn by sound.
Check yourself the next day, a week later and after a month, and ask your teacher or community to hear you.
review: Mnemos schedules checks at 1, 7, 30, 90 and 180 days for the sections you have learned. A piece that slips comes back the next day.
caveat: Mnemos is a practice aid, not religious or any other instruction. It takes no view on which text, translation, edition or manner of reciting is right: follow your teacher and your community. It cannot hear you, correct your pronunciation or melody, or check that what you typed is accurate. Communities differ on how written texts, including on a screen, should be handled. If you are unsure, ask your teacher.

title: A long poem, stanza by stanza
intro: A long poem is too much for one evening and just right for a few weeks. Learn one stanza a day, and let each day start by checking the days before.
example: Give each stanza a room and each line one picture if you like pictures, and use first letters to check yourself. Keep the first line of each stanza very clear, because it is the doorway into the stanza.
steps: Read the whole poem once for its meaning, so you know where it is going.
Learn one stanza a day, starting each day by saying the earlier stanzas from nothing.
Add the poem to Your Own Text so that the later checks are scheduled for you.
review: Checks at 1, 7, 30, 90 and 180 days, one stanza at a time.
caveat: Some learners go faster and some slower, and the right speed is the one where you can still say yesterday's stanza. Pictures hold the order of the lines. The exact words come from many checks over time.

title: Sums, squares and constants
intro: Pictures are for the numbers you need to have ready, not for the sum you are doing. For the sum, use a calculating strategy and say each partial result aloud.
example: 487 plus 356, left to right: 487 plus 300 is 787, plus 50 is 837, plus 6 is 843. For 17 squared, many people simply learn 289 by heart. For the speed of light, 299,792,458 metres a second, split it into 299, 792 and 458 and give each chunk a picture.
steps: Work left to right and say the partial results aloud, so the biggest part of the answer comes first.
Learn the facts you use often: tables to 15 by 15, squares to 30, powers of two, a few constants.
Use a picture only for a fact that keeps slipping, and keep checking it until the picture is not needed.
review: Check the fact tomorrow and again after a week. For sums, do a few a day in Mental Reckoning and look at the steps it shows.
caveat: Turning a half-finished sum into pictures usually costs more time than it saves. Fast mental calculators rely mostly on calculation methods and number facts they know by heart, built over years. Mental Reckoning practises these steps on these sums. It does not make you faster at maths in general.

title: Dates and historical events
intro: A date is a number attached to an event. The Major System gives the number two pictures, and a timeline gives the event its place.
example: 1066 is 10 and 66: toes and judge. Picture a judge with ten toes pulling an arrow from a bright eye at the first desk of a hall. The next desk holds 1215, then 1337, and the order of the desks keeps the order of the years.
steps: Pad the year to four digits and turn each pair into its Major picture.
Make one scene with the year pictures and one picture of the event, and put it on the next desk of a timeline.
Walk the desks in order, then give the year for each event from memory.
review: Check the set the next day, after a week and after a month. Years you keep mixing up deserve a stranger picture.
caveat: Pictures keep a bare year attached to an event. They do not explain why anything happened, and for years you half know already a plain check is faster. Learning dates is not the same as knowing history.

title: Facts you want to keep
intro: Quiz facts are cue and answer pairs: a question and the answer to it. They are a good place to practise the loop of picture, place, check and come back.
example: Question: who painted The Birth of Venus? Answer: Botticelli. Picture a bottle of cello music sitting in a seashell, as Venus does in the painting. Put it on a stop in your art room. Tomorrow, see if the room gives the answer before you look.
steps: Skip what you already know. Choose the facts you missed the first time you were asked.
Make one picture for each answer, joined to the question, and put it in a room for that subject.
Check from the question alone, then fix only the ones that slipped.
review: Day 1, day 7 and day 30, as for every set.
caveat: A fact you already know does not need a picture. Keep the pictures for facts that do not stay. The game's facts are public and checked, and you can trust a fact only as far as its source, so keep an eye out for updates.

title: Terms, word roots and names for a course
intro: Courses ask you to learn long lists of terms: the parts of a word, the elements, the nerves of the head, the bones of the wrist. These are lists in a set order or sets of names, which is where pictures and places help.
example: The element with number 26 is iron. The Major picture for 26 is a notch, so picture an iron nail cut into a notch. For word roots, scrib means write: picture a scribe writing on a long scroll, and then think of describe and manuscript.
steps: Pick one small set: 10 roots, 10 elements, or the cranial nerves.
Make a picture for each term and put it in a room or on a stop, in order if the order matters.
Test yourself without the book, then check yourself again later.
review: A short check at day 1, 7 and 30, and the week before the exam.
caveat: These pictures help with names and orders. They do not teach chemistry, medicine or English. Anatomy terms here are for study and not health advice. Roots give a good first guess at a new word, and guesses are sometimes wrong, so check a dictionary. Nothing here promises an exam result.

title: Countries and capitals
intro: A capital is a classic cue and answer. Give each region a room of your palace and each country one stop.
example: Hungary: picture a hungry bug (a pest) eating a flower bud. That sounds like Budapest. Put it on the first stop of your Europe room. Later, when you see Hungary in the room, the bug is there.
steps: Pick one region and about eight countries.
Make a sound-alike picture of each capital and join it to a picture of the country.
Walk the room and say each capital before you look.
review: Day 1, day 7 and day 30. Mix the region with an older one so the rooms do not blur.
caveat: Some capitals are in dispute or change, and the game keeps those out. Knowing a capital says very little about a country. Check a current atlas if it matters.

title: Music theory lists
intro: Theory has a few fixed lists: the order of sharps, the lines of a clef, the size of each interval. Pictures hold these lists. Your ears and hands do the music.
example: The order of sharps is F C G D A E B. Make a sentence: Fat Cats Grin, Dogs Always Eat Bread. The flats come in the opposite order, B E A D G C F: Bad Eggs Are Dropped, Gently Carried, Fast. Your own sentence is stronger than mine.
steps: Pick one list, such as the order of sharps or the twelve intervals.
Make a sentence or a chain of pictures, with one picture for each item.
Say the list, then check it against the book.
review: Day 1, day 7 and day 30. Use the list at your instrument the same week.
caveat: Music is learned by ear and hands. Pictures help the lists, and they do not help you play or hear better.

title: Chess openings
intro: An opening is a line of first moves. You can hold the order with pictures, and you hold the reasons only by playing and understanding the ideas.
example: The Ruy Lopez runs 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5. Picture a pawn jumping onto a tall e-door, a knight hopping after it, and a bishop pinning a note to a b-shaped board. One scene, five moves.
steps: Pick one line you actually play, no more than six moves.
Give each move one picture, and put the line on a short route.
Check the line from the first move, then play it in a game.
review: Day 1, day 7 and day 30, and after every game where you left the line.
caveat: Strong players learn openings through ideas and real games. Pictures only help you hold the order of a line you chose to learn. They do not make you better at chess.
